preamble: Vocalization of a voiced labiodental consonant to the high back rounded vowel [u] or its non-syllabic counterpart [u̯]. Friction and the labiodental contact are given up, while labiality and voicing are kept. In Slovene, syllable-initial /ʋ/ before a consonant is a full syllabic [u] for many speakers (vsi [uˈsî] 'all'), and the isolated preposition v is [úː]. In Ukrainian and Belarusian, /ʋ/ in the syllable coda is [u̯] (Belarusian writes it ⟨ў⟩: праўда 'truth'). In the history of English, Old English intervocalic [v] vocalized to the u-offglide of a diphthong after syncope, as in hafoc > Middle English hauk > hawk.

examples.note: Syllable-initial /ʋ/ before a consonant becomes a full vowel [u] for some speakers; others keep it consonantal by labializing the next consonant ([ˈʷsî]).
Within a sentence the preposition is pronounced [u̯]; cited in isolation it is a full long vowel.

examples.from: ви́вчити /ʋ/ in the coda 'to have learnt'
examples.note: In syllable codas /ʋ/ is most commonly realized as non-syllabic [u̯] (also transcribed [w]).
Word-initial /ʋ/ before a consonant is likewise non-syllabic [u̯] and alternates with syllabic /u/.
Coda /v/ is pronounced [u̯] and spelled ⟨ў⟩ (non-syllabic u).
Word-final /v/ is likewise [u̯], written ⟨ў⟩; compare Russian любовь with [f].
After the unstressed vowel was lost, the intervocalic voiced fricative [v] vocalized to [u], giving the diphthong au of Modern English hawk.
The same vocalization of [v] before a consonant after syncope; nauger was later rebracketed as an auger.

sources: Šuštaršič, R., Komar, S., & Petek, B. (1995). Slovene. Journal of the International Phonetic Association, 25(2), 86–90. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0025100300005211
